Soil that has to go

Asbestos contaminated soil removal, excavated, classified and disposed of under licence

Excavation, removal and disposal of asbestos contaminated soil. Usually the result of fibro being broken up, burnt or buried on a property decades ago, and usually found when somebody starts digging. The ground is classified before it moves, because the classification is what decides where it can legally go. Send the report or the sample results, and we will price excavation, cartage and disposal.

0456 220 552

Removal by licensed asbestos removalists. Max holds demolition licence AD214737

Before anything starts

Six things have to be settled first, and not all of them are ours

Most jobs that run late run late on this list rather than on the work itself. Each line says who owns it.

  1. 01

    Soil sampling and classification

    Who You, through an environmental consultant

    Soil is sampled and classified differently from building materials. This is what sets the disposal pathway and therefore most of the cost.

  2. 02

    Extent of the contamination

    Who Your consultant

    How far it goes laterally and how deep. Without this the excavation has no defined edge.

  3. 03

    Validation plan agreed

    Who You, through your consultant

    How the site will be shown to be clean once the material is out. Agree it before digging.

  4. 04

    Licensed removalist engaged

    Who Max

    Asbestos contaminated soil is handled under the asbestos pathway, not as general excavation.

  5. 05

    Disposal facility booked

    Who Max

    A facility licensed to receive the specific classification, confirmed before the first load.

  6. 06

    Controls for the open excavation

    Who Max

    Dust suppression, exclusion zones and covering, because an open contaminated pit is a live risk.

The detail

What makes contaminated soil so much more expensive than sheeting

  • It is priced by the tonne, not by the sheet. Soil is heavy. A small area of contamination can be a large tonnage once it is excavated to depth.
  • The classification sets the destination. A facility licensed for that classification, which is often not the closest one, and the cartage distance is part of the price.
  • The extent is unknown until it is sampled. Which is why an honest quote prices the excavation and disposal on rates rather than a fixed figure.
  • The hole cannot close until it is validated. Backfilling before your consultant has taken their samples means digging it out again.
  • Water finds the pit. An open excavation collects water, and that water is usually classified too.
  • The report outlives the job. The validation report is what a future purchaser, certifier or lender will ask for.

What we need to quote it

The address
So we can look at access and what is around it
Photographs
One from the street and one of the work itself
Any reports you hold
Hazardous materials, structural, survey or levels
Your dates
What has to be finished by when, and what is waiting on it

We attend the site before quoting anything substantial.

Found fibro fragments while digging?

Stop the excavation and leave the material in place. Continuing to dig spreads the contamination and turns a defined area into an undefined one.

Before you book

What people ask about this one

How did asbestos get into the soil?
Usually because fibro was broken up, burnt or buried on the property decades ago, back when that was ordinary practice. It also happens where a previous demolition was done badly.
Can you give a fixed price?
Not honestly, until the ground is classified and the extent is known. The excavation and disposal are priced on rates agreed before we start, so the exposure is visible rather than hidden inside a contingency you pay for either way.
Who does the classification?
An environmental consultant, engaged by you. It is deliberately not us: the person who defines how much has to come out should not be the person paid to take it out.
What happens to the hole?
Once your consultant has taken validation samples and is satisfied, it is backfilled with clean fill or VENM and compacted in layers. That is a separate scope and a separate line.
Does this stop my build?
It delays it, and finding it early is far better than finding it late. The worst version is discovering it after footings are in.

The classification and the extent are what make this quotable. If you do not have them yet, tell us what was found and we will tell you what the next step is.
